title: Pork adobo
intro: Pork belly braised in soy sauce, vinegar, garlic and bay leaves until the meat is tender and the fat turns soft and rich. The sauce is salty, sharp and garlicky, made for spooning over plenty of rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the pork in batches until the edges are golden and some fat has rendered.
Pour off all but about 1 tablespoon of the fat. Lower the heat to medium and fry the garlic until fragrant and pale gold.
Return the pork to the pot with the soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns. Bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring so its raw edge cooks off.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until a fork slides easily into the pork. Stir now and then and add a splash of water if the pot looks dry.
Uncover, stir in the sugar if using, and simmer until the sauce has reduced and the pork looks glossy.
Taste and adjust with a little more vinegar or water. Remove the bay leaves and serve with rice.

tips: For deeper flavor, marinate the pork in the soy sauce and half the garlic overnight in the fridge before cooking. Skim some fat off the top before serving if you like a lighter sauce.

title: Chicken and pork adobo
intro: Pork belly and chicken cooked together in one pot of soy sauce, vinegar and garlic, so the pork fat enriches the sauce and the chicken soaks it all up. A big, generous adobo for family meals.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the pork until golden on most sides, then set it aside.
Brown the chicken skin side down in the pork fat, in batches if needed, and set it aside.
Lower the heat to medium and fry the garlic in the fat until fragrant and just golden.
Return only the pork to the pot. Add the soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns and bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer the pork on low heat to give it a head start, since it takes longer than the chicken.
Add the chicken, cover again and simmer until both meats are tender, turning the pieces once.
Uncover, stir in the sugar if using, and simmer until the sauce is reduced and coats the meat.
Taste, adjust with vinegar or water, remove the bay leaves and serve with rice.

tips: Pork shoulder (kasim) works in place of belly for a leaner pot. The leftovers make excellent adobo flakes or fried rice.

title: Adobong puti
intro: Adobo made without soy sauce: pork simmered in vinegar, salt, garlic and pepper, then browned in its own rendered fat. It comes out pale, tangy and very garlicky, with crisp golden edges.

steps.text: Put the pork, half the garlic, the salt, peppercorns, bay leaves and water in a heavy pot. Pour the vinegar over the top.
Bring to a boil over medium-high heat and let it boil without stirring.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the pork is tender.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and keep cooking, stirring now and then, until the liquid has evaporated and the pork starts to fry in its own fat.
Push the pork to one side, add the oil and the rest of the garlic, and fry the garlic until golden. Toss everything together and keep frying until the pork edges are browned.
Taste for salt and serve hot with rice.

tips: Use a good cane or coconut vinegar here since there is no soy sauce to round it out. A spoonful of vinegar with crushed garlic on the side makes a good dip.

title: Adobong dilaw
intro: Chicken adobo colored and flavored with fresh turmeric instead of soy sauce, so the sauce turns bright yellow, tangy and gently earthy. The chicken is browned at the end for a little crispness.

items.name: fresh turmeric (luyang dilaw)
items.note: peeled and grated, or 1 tbsp ground turmeric

steps.text: Put the chicken, turmeric, ginger, half the garlic, salt, peppercorns, bay leaves and water in a pot. Pour the vinegar over.
Bring to a boil and let it boil without stirring.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the chicken is cooked through and tender.
Lift the chicken out. Boil the sauce uncovered until reduced by about half.
In a pan, heat the oil and fry the remaining garlic until golden. Add the chicken and brown it lightly on both sides.
Pour the reduced sauce over the chicken, let it bubble for a minute, taste for salt and serve with rice.

tips: Fresh turmeric stains hands, boards and plastic: wear gloves or grate it straight into the pot.

title: Chicken adobo sa gata
intro: Chicken adobo finished with coconut milk, which turns the sharp, salty sauce creamy, rich and mellow. Long green chilies add a mild heat.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium-high heat and brown the chicken skin side down. Set aside.
Lower the heat to medium and saute the garlic and onion until soft and fragrant.
Return the chicken with the soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns. Bring to a boil, pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer until the chicken is tender.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer uncovered, stirring now and then, until the sauce thickens and a little oil shows on the surface.
Add the green chilies and cook until just softened.
Taste, adjust with salt or a splash of vinegar, and serve with rice.

tips: Keep the heat at a gentle simmer once the coconut milk goes in so it does not curdle. Add a few siling labuyo with the green chilies if you want it hot.

title: Pork adobo sa gata
intro: Pork adobo that is reduced until the meat fries in its own fat, then simmered in coconut milk with plenty of siling labuyo. Rich, creamy and properly spicy.

steps.text: Put the pork, half the garlic, soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns in a heavy pot. Bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the pork is tender.
Uncover and cook on medium heat, stirring often, until the liquid is gone and the pork starts to fry in its rendered fat.
Add the remaining garlic, the onion and ginger and fry with the pork until fragrant.
Pour in the coconut milk and add the siling labuyo. Simmer uncovered, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and oily.
Add the green chilies and cook until bright and just tender. Taste for salt and serve with rice.

tips: Seed the siling labuyo, or use fewer, if you are cooking for kids. Like any adobo it tastes better the next day.

title: Adobong tuyo
intro: Dry adobo: pork cooked in soy sauce and vinegar until every drop of sauce is gone, then fried in its own fat until dark, sticky and crisp at the edges. Intense, salty and best with plain rice and tomatoes.

items.name: pork shoulder (kasim)
items.note: cut into 1-inch cubes, with some fat

steps.text: Combine the pork, soy sauce, water, half the garlic, bay leaves and peppercorns in a wide pan. Bring to a boil.
Add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer on low heat until the pork is tender.
Uncover, add the sugar if using, and cook on medium heat, stirring often, until the sauce has completely evaporated.
Add the oil and the remaining garlic. Fry, stirring and scraping the pan, until the pork is dark, sticky and crisp at the edges.
Remove the bay leaves and serve with rice and sliced tomatoes.

tips: Stir constantly during the last few minutes: the sugars in the soy sauce go from caramelized to burnt quickly. It keeps well for packed lunches since there is no sauce to spill.

title: Crispy adobo
intro: Pork belly slabs braised in adobo sauce until tender, then deep-fried until the skin and edges are crackling. Served chopped with the reduced sauce for dipping.

steps.text: Put the pork, soy sauce, water, garlic, bay leaves and peppercorns in a pot and bring to a boil. Add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer on low heat until the pork is tender but still holds its shape.
Lift out the pork and pat it very dry with paper towels. Let it sit on a rack to air-dry while you reduce the sauce.
Boil the braising liquid uncovered until reduced to about half a cup. Strain it into a dipping bowl.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to about 175°C (350°F). Fry the pork, skin side down first, until deep golden and crisp all over. Use a splatter guard or lid held at an angle.
Drain on a rack and rest briefly, then chop into bite-size pieces.
Serve with the reduced sauce for dipping and steamed rice.

tips: Any water left on the pork makes the oil spit hard, so dry it well. You can braise the pork a day ahead and fry it straight from the fridge.

title: Adobo flakes
intro: Chicken adobo shredded and fried until crisp, then tossed with reduced adobo sauce and toasted garlic. Salty, crunchy and great with garlic rice, eggs or in pandesal.

steps.text: Put the chicken, soy sauce, water, crushed garlic, bay leaves and peppercorns in a pot. Bring to a boil, add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer until the chicken is very tender.
Lift out the chicken and let it cool enough to handle.
Meanwhile, boil the sauce uncovered until reduced to about one third of a cup. Strain and set aside.
Discard the skin and bones and shred the chicken into thin strands with two forks or your fingers.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Fry the minced garlic until golden, then scoop it out with a slotted spoon.
Fry the shredded chicken in the same oil in batches, stirring often, until browned and crisp.
Return all the chicken to the pan, pour in the reduced sauce and keep stirring until it is absorbed and the flakes crisp up again.
Toss with the fried garlic and drain on paper towels. Let cool before storing.

tips: Adobo flakes keep for a week in a clean jar in the fridge. Re-crisp them in a dry pan before serving.

title: Pineapple chicken adobo
intro: Chicken adobo simmered with pineapple juice and chunks, so the sauce turns sweet, tangy and sticky. Kids usually love this one.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium-high heat and brown the chicken skin side down. Set aside.
Saute the garlic and onion in the same pot until soft.
Return the chicken and add the soy sauce, 1 cup of the reserved pineapple juice (top up with water if short), the bay leaves and pepper. Bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer until the chicken is tender.
Add the pineapple chunks and simmer uncovered until the sauce is reduced and syrupy.
Taste, adjust with a splash of vinegar if too sweet, and serve with rice.

tips: Fresh pineapple works too: use about 2 cups of chunks and 1 cup of water with a tablespoon of brown sugar in place of the canned juice.

title: Chicken adobo with potatoes
intro: Everyday chicken adobo stretched with fried potatoes that soak up the salty, tangy sauce. A filling, budget-friendly pot for a big family.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium heat and fry the potatoes until golden on the outside. Set aside.
Raise the heat and brown the chicken skin side down in the same oil. Set aside.
Lower the heat and fry the garlic until fragrant.
Return the chicken with the soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns. Bring to a boil, add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer.
Add the potatoes, cover again and simmer until both chicken and potatoes are tender.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce is slightly reduced. Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: Frying the potatoes first keeps them from breaking up in the sauce. Hard-boiled eggs can go in with the potatoes for an even heartier pot.

title: Pork adobo with eggs
intro: Pork adobo with hard-boiled eggs simmered in the sauce until they turn brown and salty all the way through. One egg per person stretches the meat further.

steps.text: Put the eggs in a pot of cold water, bring to a boil and cook. Cool in cold water and peel.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the pork in batches.
Lower the heat and fry the garlic until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns and bring to a boil. Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer until the pork is almost tender.
Add the peeled eggs and sugar. Simmer uncovered, turning the eggs now and then, until they are evenly browned and the sauce has reduced.
Taste, adjust and serve with rice, halving the eggs at the table.

tips: Prick each peeled egg a few times with a toothpick so the sauce seeps in faster.

title: Adobong pakpak
intro: Chicken wings browned and cooked in a slightly sweet adobo sauce that is reduced until sticky and clings to the wings. Good with rice or as pulutan.

items.name: chicken wings
items.note: split at the joints, tips discarded

steps.text: Pat the wings dry. Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and brown the wings on both sides, in batches if needed.
Push the wings aside and fry the garlic until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar, bay leaves and pepper and bring to a boil. Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer until the wings are tender.
Uncover, raise the heat and cook, turning the wings often, until the sauce is thick and sticky and coats them.
Remove the bay leaves and serve hot.

tips: Watch the pan closely at the end: once the sauce turns syrupy it can scorch within a minute.

title: Adobong paa ng manok
intro: Chicken feet simmered slowly in soy sauce, vinegar and garlic until the skin turns soft and sticky. A cheap, flavorful favorite with rice or as pulutan.

steps.text: Rub the chicken feet with the salt, rinse well and snip off the nails with kitchen shears. Peel off any yellow skin that remains.
Blanch the feet in a pot of boiling water, then drain and rinse.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the chicken feet, soy sauce, water, bay leaves, peppercorns and sugar. Bring to a boil, pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer on low heat until the skin is soft and starts to pull away from the bones. Add water if the pot gets dry.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce is thick and glossy, stirring so the feet do not stick.
Add the chilies if using, cook for a minute, and serve.

tips: A pressure cooker cuts the simmering time to about 20 minutes; reduce the sauce afterward with the lid off.

title: Pork spareribs adobo
intro: Pork spareribs browned and braised low and slow in adobo sauce until the meat pulls cleanly off the bone. The bones give the sauce extra body and flavor.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the ribs well on all sides in batches. Set aside.
Pour off excess fat, lower the heat and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Return the ribs with the soy sauce, water, bay leaves, peppercorns and sugar. Bring to a boil, add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer on low heat until the meat is very tender and pulls away from the bones. Turn the ribs every 20 minutes and add water if needed.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce is reduced and sticky.
Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: Ask the butcher to cut the ribs into short pieces across the bone so they fit in the pot and cook evenly.

title: Adobong tenga ng baboy
intro: Pig ears boiled until tender, sliced thin and tossed in a garlicky adobo sauce with chilies. Chewy and crunchy at once, and a favorite pulutan.

steps.text: Scrape the pig ears with a knife and singe off any hairs over a flame. Rinse well.
Boil the ears in the water with the salt and bay leaves, covered, until a fork goes in easily.
Drain, let cool, then slice into thin strips.
Heat the oil in a pan and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the sliced ears, soy sauce, water and pepper and simmer.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring.
Cook, stirring, until most of the sauce is absorbed. Add the chilies, toss and serve.

tips: Boiling the ears a day ahead makes this a quick dish. A pressure cooker gets them tender in about 25 minutes.

title: Beef adobo
intro: Beef chuck or brisket braised for a couple of hours in soy sauce, vinegar and garlic until it is fork-tender. The sauce turns deep, dark and beefy.

steps.text: Pat the beef dry. Heat the oil in a heavy pot over high heat and brown the beef in batches. Set aside.
Lower the heat to medium and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Return the beef with the soy sauce, water, bay leaves, peppercorns and sugar. Bring to a boil, pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer on low heat until the beef is fork-tender. Check every 30 minutes and add hot water if the liquid drops below the meat.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce has reduced and coats the beef.
Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: A pressure cooker gets the beef tender in about 35 minutes. Lean cuts like sirloin dry out here; choose a cut with some fat and connective tissue.

title: Adobong kambing
intro: Goat meat parboiled with ginger, then braised in a sharp, peppery adobo until tender. The vinegar and ginger tame the strong flavor of the meat.

steps.text: Put the goat and the crushed ginger in a pot, cover with water and bring to a boil. Boil, then drain and rinse off the scum.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the goat pieces.
Add the garlic, onion and ginger strips and saute until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns and bring to a boil. Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer on low heat until the goat is tender, adding hot water as needed.
Uncover, add the chilies if using, and simmer until the sauce is reduced and thick.
Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: Goat varies a lot in toughness: older goat can need up to an hour more. A pressure cooker brings it to tender in about 40 minutes.

title: Adobong pato
intro: Duck pieces browned in their own fat, then braised in soy sauce, vinegar, garlic and ginger until tender. Richer and gamier than chicken adobo, with a deep, glossy sauce.

steps.text: Pat the duck dry. Lay the pieces skin side down in a cold, dry heavy pot, then turn the heat to medium. Cook until the skin is golden and much of the fat has rendered, turning once.
Remove the duck and pour off all but 2 tablespoons of fat. Saute the garlic, ginger and onion until fragrant.
Return the duck with the soy sauce, water, bay leaves, peppercorns and sugar. Bring to a boil, add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer on low heat until the duck is tender, turning the pieces now and then.
Uncover, skim off excess fat and simmer until the sauce is reduced and glossy.
Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: Save the rendered duck fat in a jar in the fridge: it makes very good fried rice.

title: Adobong atay at balunbalunan
intro: Chicken gizzards simmered until tender in adobo sauce, with chicken livers added at the end so they stay soft and creamy. Cheap, rich and very good with rice.

steps.text: Trim the gizzards of any tough yellow lining and fat, and trim the livers of any green spots. Rinse both and keep them separate.
Heat the oil in a pot and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the gizzards, soy sauce, water, bay leaves and pepper and bring to a boil. Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer until the gizzards are tender.
Add the livers and simmer uncovered, stirring gently, until they are just cooked through and no longer pink inside.
Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: Do not overcook the livers or they turn grainy and bitter: pull the pot off the heat as soon as they are just done.

title: Adobong palaka
intro: Frog legs fried until golden, then simmered briefly in a garlicky adobo sauce. The meat is mild, tender and a little like chicken.

steps.text: Rinse the frog legs, pat them dry and season with the salt.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and fry the frog legs in batches until light golden. Set aside.
Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of oil. Saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Return the frog legs with the soy sauce, water, bay leaves and pepper. Bring to a boil, add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Simmer uncovered, turning the legs gently, until the sauce is reduced and coats them.
Add the chilies if using and serve with rice.

tips: Buy frog legs already cleaned and skinned from the wet market. Frying first keeps the delicate meat from falling apart in the sauce.

title: Adobo fried rice
intro: Leftover pork or chicken adobo shredded and fried with day-old rice, lots of garlic and a splash of adobo sauce. Salty, garlicky and a one-pan breakfast or lunch.

steps.text: Break up any clumps in the rice with your hands.
Heat the oil in a wok or wide pan over medium heat. Fry the garlic until golden, then scoop out half for topping.
Add the shredded adobo and fry until the edges are browned and crisp.
Add the rice and adobo sauce and toss over high heat until the rice is hot and the grains are separate.
Push the rice to one side, pour in the eggs and scramble until just set, then mix through the rice.
Season with salt and pepper, toss in the green onions and serve topped with the reserved garlic.

tips: Freshly cooked rice turns mushy; if that is all you have, spread it on a tray and let it cool and dry for an hour first.

title: Adobosilog
intro: A breakfast plate of leftover adobo fried until browned, garlic fried rice and a sunny-side-up egg. Salty, garlicky and very filling.

steps.text: Put the garlic and oil in a cold pan, then heat over medium-low until the garlic is golden. Scoop out half the garlic for topping.
Add the rice and salt to the pan and toss until the rice is hot and slightly toasty. Keep warm and top with the reserved garlic.
In another pan, heat the oil. Separate the adobo pieces from the sauce and fry them until the edges are browned. Pour in the sauce and let it bubble until thick.
Wipe the pan, heat the oil for the eggs and fry them sunny side up until the whites are set and the edges are crisp.
Plate the rice, adobo and eggs together with the tomato and a small bowl of spiced vinegar.

tips: Leftover adobo that has sat in the fridge overnight fries up best, since the sauce has thickened and the meat is firm.
